source_text: Οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ μακαριότης ψυχῆς κεχωρισμένης σώματος· οὐδὲ γὰρ τὴν θατέρου τούτων ἐξ ὦν συνέστηκεν ἄνθρωπος ἐσκοποῦμεν ζωὴν ἢ τέλος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ συνεστῶτος ἐξ ἀμφοῖν· τοιοῦτος γὰρ πᾶς ὁ τόνδε τὸν βίον λαχὼν ἄνθρωπος, καὶ δεῖ τῆς τούτου ζωῆς εἶναί τι τέλος οἰκεῖον. Εἰ δὲ τοῦ συναμφοτέρου τὸ τέλος, τοῦτο δὲ οὔτε ζώντων αὐτῶν ἔτι κατὰ τόνδε τὸν βίον εὑρεθῆναι δυνατὸν διὰ τὰς πολλάκις ἤδη ῥηθείσας αἰτίας, οὔτε μὴν ἐν χωρισμῷ τυγχανούσης τῆς ψυχῆς, τῷ μηδὲ συνεστάναι τὸν τοιοῦτον ἄνθρωπον διαλυθέντος ἢ καὶ πάντη σκεδασθέντος τοῦ σώματος, κἂν ἡ ψυχὴ διαμένῃ καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν, ἀνάγκη πᾶσα κατ᾿ ἄλλην τινὰ τοῦ συναμφοτέρου καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ζώου σύστασιν τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων φανῆναι τέλος. Τούτου δ᾿ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἑπομένου, δεῖ πάντως γενέσθαι τῶν νεκρωθέντων ἢ καὶ πάντη διαλυθέντων σωμάτων ἀνάστασιν καὶ τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἀνθρώπους συστῆναι πάλιν· ἐπειδή γε τὸ μὲν τέλος οὐχ ἁπλῶς, οὐδὲ τῶν ἐπιτυχόντων ἀνθρώπων, ὁ τῆς φύσεως τίθεται νόμος, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐκείνων τῶν κατὰ τὴν προλαβοῦσαν ζωὴν βεβιωκότων, τοὺς δ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἀνθρώπους συστῆναι πάλιν ἀμήχανον, μὴ τῶν αὐτῶν σωμάτων ταῖς αὐταῖς ψυχαῖς ἀποδοθέντων. Τὸ δ᾿ αὐτὸ σῶμα τὴν αὐτὴν ψυχὴν ἀπολαβεῖν ἄλλως μὲν ἀδύνατον, κατὰ μόνην δὲ τὴν ἀνάστασιν δυνατόν· ταύτης γὰρ γενομένης καὶ τὸ τῇ φύσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρόσφορον ἐπακολουθεῖ τέλος. Τέλος δὲ ζωῆς ἔμφρονος καὶ λογικῆς κρίσεως οὐκ ἂν ἁμάρτοι τις εἰπὼν τὸ τούτοις ἀπερισπάστως συνδιαιωνίζειν οἷς μάλιστα καὶ πρώτως ὁ φυσικὸς συνήρμοσται λόγος, τῇ τε θεωρίᾳ τοῦ ὄντος καὶ τῶν ἐκεὶνῳ δεδογμένων ἀπαύστως ἐπαγάλλεσθαι· κἂν οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐμπαθέστερον καὶ σφοδρότερον τοῖς τῇδε προσπεπονθότες ἄστοχοι τούτου διατελῶσιν. Οὐ γὰρ ἀκυροῖ τὴν κοινὴν ἀποκλήρωσιν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἀποπιπτόντων τοῦ προσήκοντος αὐτοῖς τέλους, ἰδιαζούσης τῆς ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐξετάσεως καὶ τῆς ἑκάστῳ συμμετρουμένης ὑπὲρ τῶν εὗ ἢ κακῶς βεβιωμένων τιμῆς ἢ δίκης.
pass_a_gloss: Not indeed also happiness of soul separated from body; for we do not consider life or end of one of these from which man consists, but of the one consisting of both; for every man having obtained this life here is such, and it is necessary for this life to be some end proper to it. But if the end is of the one consisting of both, this is not possible to be found while they are still living in this life, because of the many causes already spoken, nor indeed when the soul is in separation, since the man of such a kind does not consist with the body having been dissolved or even completely scattered, even if the soul remains by itself, it is necessary for the end of men to appear in some other constitution of the one consisting of both and of the same living being. This being necessarily the case, it is necessary for the bodies of those who have died or even been completely dissolved to rise again and for the same men to be constituted again; since the law of nature sets the end not simply, nor of men who happen to exist, but of those very ones who have lived according to the life before, and it is impossible for the same men to be constituted again unless the same bodies are given back to the same souls. For the same body to receive the same soul is impossible in any other way, but possible according to the resurrection alone; for when this happens, the end suitable to the nature of men follows. And the end of a life with understanding and rational judgment would not be mistaken if someone were to say it is to live together with those things with which the natural reason is most and first harmonized, to rejoice constantly in the contemplation of what exists and the things given to it, even if many men, being more intensely and violently affected by the things here, miss this; for the multitude of those falling away from the end proper to them does not invalidate the common judgment, with the examination of these things being private and the honor or justice measured out to each for the things well or badly lived.

choices.english: the end suitable to the nature of men
choices.term: τὸ τῇ φύσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρόσφορον

pass_b_english: Happiness does not belong to a soul separated from the body either; we do not look for life or an end in one of the two components from which man consists, but in the composite made of both. Every man who has obtained this life here is of that sort, and his life must have some proper end. But if the end belongs to the composite, it cannot be found while they are still living in this life, for the many causes already stated, nor yet when the soul is in separation, since such a man ceases to consist when the body has been dissolved or even completely scattered, even if the soul remains by itself. Necessity therefore demands that the end of men appear in some other constitution of the same composite, the same living being. Since this follows necessarily, the bodies of those who have died or been completely dissolved must rise again, and the same men must be constituted once more. For the law of nature sets the end not simply, nor for men who happen to exist, but for those very ones who have lived according to the preceding life, and it is impossible for the same men to be constituted again unless the same bodies are given back to the same souls. The same body can receive the same soul in no other way, but only through the resurrection; when this happens, the end fitting to the nature of men follows. One would not misspeak in saying that the end of a life of understanding and rational judgment is to live together without distraction with those things with which natural reason is most and first harmonized, to rejoice unceasingly in the contemplation of being and the things given to it, even though many men, affected more intensely and violently by the things here, continue to miss this. The multitude of those falling away from the end proper to them does not invalidate the common lot, since the examination of these things is private and the honor or justice measured out to each for things well or badly lived is proportioned.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional and causal structures of the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source. The distinction between the composite nature of man and the necessity of bodily resurrection is preserved. All clauses, including the nuances of 'the same bodies given back to the same souls' (τοὺς αὐτῶν σωμάτων ταῖς αὐταῖς ψυχαῖς ἀποδοθέντων) and the final clause regarding individual justice, are correctly rendered.
